Greedy equivalence search on the residual covariance

Source: R/ges.R
mc_ges.Rd

Searches over Markov equivalence classes of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) by the two-phase greedy equivalence search (GES) of Chickering (2002): a forward phase that starts from the empty class (or from start) and applies, at each step, the insertion that raises the score most, and a backward phase that starts from what the forward phase left and applies the best deletion. Each phase stops when no operator improves the score. The score of a class, computed through any of its members, is the penalized Gaussian working criterion $$\sum_{j=1}^{R}\left\{-\frac{n}{2}\log\hat\delta_j- \frac{\lambda}{2}\,(|P_j|+1)\right\},$$ where \(\hat\delta_j\) is the residual variance of the regression of response \(j\) on its parents \(P_j\) in the residual covariance (the closed-form innovation variance of the directed layer), \(|P_j|+1\) counts the coefficients and the innovation variance of the node, and \(\lambda\) is the penalty. Larger is better. Up to an additive constant the score is \(-1/2\) times the criterion \(-2\ell^p_e+\lambda q\), with \(\ell^p_e\) the maximized working criterion and \(q=R+|E|\) the number of parameters of the member, so that maximizing it with \(\lambda=\log n\) minimizes the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) of the working criterion. A parent set whose block of the residual covariance is numerically singular, or that leaves a nonpositive residual variance, scores -Inf and is never chosen.

Usage

mc_ges(fit, penalty = NULL, start = NULL, max_set = 12L, max_steps = 200L)

# S3 method for class 'mcg_ges'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

fit

an object of class "mcglm_graph", whose residual covariance the search runs on.

penalty

single finite non-negative number, the multiplier \(\lambda\) on the parameter count. NULL (default) uses log(n), with n the number of units of the fit, which is the Bayesian information criterion; 2 gives Akaike's.

start

optional square 0/1 adjacency matrix on the responses, in the package convention, to start the forward phase from; it should be a CPDAG. The default is the empty class.

max_set

largest number of candidate neighbors enumerated by an operator (a node pair whose candidate set is larger is skipped), a guard against the exponential growth in dense neighborhoods. A single non-negative integer.

max_steps

cap on the number of steps of each phase, a single positive integer.

x

an object of class "mcg_ges".

...

ignored.

Value

An object of class "mcg_ges": a list with the cpdag adjacency matrix (labeled by response); its score; the penalty and n used; steps, a named integer vector with the number of forward and backward steps; and trace, a data frame with one row per operator applied (phase, step, the nodes x and y, the set set of neighbors involved, comma separated, and the score gain). response_names is also recorded. The print method returns x invisibly.

Why a search over classes is well posed here

The working criterion of the residual layer depends on the data through the residual covariance alone, so two members of an equivalence class fit the same covariance with the same number of parameters and score alike. That is score equivalence, and without it a search over classes would not be defined. It also means the output is a class and not a graph: what the second-order separations identify is what the score can distinguish. The score is also decomposable, a sum of terms that each depend on one node and its parents, which is what lets an operator be scored locally. The large-sample optimality of the search shown by Chickering (2002) requires in addition a locally consistent score, a property that is not claimed for the working criterion on Pearson residuals.

How it differs from the constraint-based route

mc_graph_pipeline tests separations one at a time at a fixed level and then orients; this one trades every edge against a penalty on the number of parameters and never tests a hypothesis. The two answer the same question by different means and need not agree, which is the point of having both. Neither is run through an external library.

References

Chickering, D. M. (2002). Optimal structure identification with greedy search. Journal of Machine Learning Research 3, 507-554.

See also

mc_graph_pipeline for the constraint-based route, mc_class_members to enumerate the DAGs of the class found.

Other structure discovery: mc_find_vstructures(), mc_graph_pipeline(), mc_orient_meek(), mc_pc_skeleton(), mc_residual_df(), mc_separating_sets(), mc_skeleton_to_bnlearn()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1); n <- 600; x <- rnorm(n)
z1 <- rnorm(n); z2 <- rnorm(n); z3 <- 0.8 * z1 + 0.8 * z2 + rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(y1 = z1, y2 = z2, y3 = z3, x = x)
f <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x), data = d)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
mc_ges(f)
#> Greedy equivalence search (penalty = 6.4, n = 600)
#> Steps: 2 forward, 0 backward | score: 270.6351
#> Skeleton edges: 2
#> Adjacency:
#>    y1 y2 y3
#> y1  0  0  1
#> y2  0  0  1
#> y3  0  0  0
# }
